1	# Phase 5 decision memo — analytics + taper mode
2	
3	(Supersedes the Phase 4 memo. Prior memos preserved in git history.)
4	
5	## Goal
6	Take everything that is already true *within one session* — per-cue RT, false-start /
7	hesitation rates, best-10 RT, anti-rhythm — and project it *across sessions* so the
8	athlete can see whether they are getting better, worse, or stagnating in the two
9	weeks before competition. Plus: a "taper mode" that uses that history to
10	auto-generate a low-volume profile that drills only the cues the athlete is
11	slowest or least accurate on.
12	
13	## Phase 5 acceptance criteria (from `docs/PHASES.md`)
14	
15	1. App shows reaction time by cue type (across sessions).
16	2. App shows false-start rate over time.
17	3. App shows hesitation rate over time.
18	4. App shows best-10-rep average and trend.
19	5. Taper mode profile: short rounds, low total volume, only the cues you are
20	   slowest or least accurate on.
21	6. Session-over-session comparison view.
22	
23	## Non-goals (Phase 5)
24	- Video opponent clips (Phase 6).
25	- Webcam pose detection (Phase 7).
26	- Cross-session storage migration — Phase 4 data model already supports it.
27	- Chart library — keep dependencies as-is; render trends with text rows + tiny
28	  inline SVG sparklines.
29	- Cloud sync / export polish (CSV/JSON export is listed as MVP feature 10 and
30	  remains deferred; analytics work here uses the data already in IndexedDB).
31	
32	## Key decisions
33	
34	### D1. Pure analytics module, separate from drill engine
35	- New file `app/src/engine/analytics.ts`.
36	- All Phase 5 aggregation functions are pure: input is `SessionRecord[]` and/or
37	  `RepRecord[]`; output is plain data structures.
38	- Keeps `drill.ts` focused on the *real-time* path (cue picking, classification,
39	  per-session summarize/cueBreakdown/antiRhythmSignal). Cross-session math is
40	  a different concern with a different read pattern (bulk-fetch from Dexie) and
41	  different lifecycle (read-only views, no orchestration).
42	- Mirrors Phase 4 style: `summarize`, `cueBreakdown`, `antiRhythmSignal` are
43	  already pure in drill.ts. We extend the same pattern, not the same file.
44	
45	Exports:
46	```ts
47	export interface SessionTrendPoint {
48	  sessionId: string
49	  startedAt: number
50	  reps: number
51	  falseStartRate: number       // false_starts / total reps
52	  hesitationRate: number       // hesitations / total reps
53	  lateRate: number             // late / total reps (go cues only denominator)
54	  avgRtMs: number | null
55	  best10AvgRtMs: number | null
56	  score: number
57	}
58	export interface CueTrendPoint {
59	  sessionId: string
60	  startedAt: number
61	  cueId: CueId
62	  reps: number
63	  avgRtMs: number | null
64	  errorRate: number            // (1 - correct/reps) for that cue
65	}
66	export interface CueAggregate {
67	  cueId: CueId
68	  reps: number                 // across sessions
69	  avgRtMs: number | null
70	  best10AvgRtMs: number | null
71	  errorRate: number
72	  weakness: number             // bigger = worse; see D5
73	}
74	export interface SessionDelta {
75	  baseline: SessionTrendPoint
76	  candidate: SessionTrendPoint
77	  deltaAvgRtMs: number | null
78	  deltaScore: number
79	  deltaFalseStartRate: number
80	  deltaHesitationRate: number
81	  perCue: { cueId: CueId; deltaAvgRtMs: number | null; deltaErrorRate: number }[]
82	}
83	export interface TaperRecommendation {
84	  cueIds: CueId[]
85	  reason: string
86	}
87	
88	export function sessionTrend(sessions: SessionRecord[], repsBySessionId: Map<string, RepRecord[]>): SessionTrendPoint[]
89	export function cueTrend(sessions: SessionRecord[], repsBySessionId: Map<string, RepRecord[]>): CueTrendPoint[]
90	export function cueAggregate(allReps: RepRecord[]): CueAggregate[]
91	export function compareSessions(a: SessionTrendPoint, b: SessionTrendPoint, aReps: RepRecord[], bReps: RepRecord[]): SessionDelta
92	export function pickTaperCues(aggregate: CueAggregate[], k: number): TaperRecommendation
93	```
94	
95	Rationale for shape: the UI wants both per-session-per-cue series (for the
96	"RT by cue type over time" view — one line per cue, X axis = session index)
97	and per-session aggregates (for the four overall trend rows). Functions take
98	the data already pre-grouped so they remain trivially testable.
99	
100	### D2. Storage read helper
101	- New helper in `app/src/store/db.ts`:
102	  - `listRepsForSessions(sessionIds: string[]): Promise<Map<string, RepRecord[]>>`
103	    uses the existing `reps.sessionId` Dexie index and groups by sessionId in
104	    a single `where('sessionId').anyOf(...)` query.
105	- No schema change. No new Dexie version.
106	- Existing `listRecentSessions(limit = 20)` is the source of "last N sessions"
107	  for the analytics view; we extend it by accepting a higher limit if needed
108	  but default to 20 (still cheap, IndexedDB returns under a few KB).
109	- Existing Phase 4 sessions persist `summary` (a `SessionSummary` snapshot).
110	  Analytics relies on the *raw reps* not on that summary, so older sessions
111	  with slightly different scoring weights still display consistently in the
112	  trend view (the summary's `score` *does* reflect that session's weights,
113	  which is the right thing — it represents what the user actually saw).
114	
115	### D3. Best-10 aggregation across sessions
116	- Two interpretations are valid:
117	  (a) "best-10 within each session, then plot the per-session best-10 as a
118	      trend point" — answers "are my fastest reps in a session improving?"
119	  (b) "best-10 across the entire history window" — answers "what's my current
120	      ceiling, full stop?"
121	- Choose **(a)** for the time-series view (the spec line is *"best-10-rep
122	  average and trend"* — singular per session, plural trend). Choose (b) for
123	  the Per-Cue Aggregate panel that drives taper-mode picking.
124	- Both share one helper: `best10AvgOf(times: number[])` → average of the 10
125	  smallest correct_go RT values (fewer if fewer reps).
126	
127	### D4. False-start and hesitation rates
128	- Denominator = *all reps in the session*. The spec talks about overall rates
129	  and trends; not normalizing to go-cue-only keeps the number directly
130	  comparable to a casual viewer.
131	- "lateRate" is included on the trend point for completeness but is not
132	  required by Phase 5 acceptance — keeping it costs us nothing and means the
133	  Phase 4 summary can re-use the same trend point shape later.
134	- Anti-rhythm narrative line stays per-session (Phase 4) — surfacing
135	  cross-session anti-rhythm patterns is genuinely noisy and is not requested
136	  by the spec.
137	
138	### D5. Weakness scoring for taper-cue picking — go and no-go scored separately
139	
140	Red-team flagged that a single weakness number conflates two things that
141	shouldn't merge:
142	- Go cues: weakness is primarily a *speed* problem — `avgRtMs` is the signal,
143	  with `errorRate` (false-start + late + hesitation, divided by reps for that
144	  cue) as a tiebreaker.
145	- No-go cues: there is no RT — `avgRtMs` is structurally `null`. Weakness is
146	  *only* the false-start rate.
147	
148	So:
149	```ts
150	interface CueAggregate {
151	  cueId: CueId
152	  isGo: boolean            // taken from CUE_LIBRARY at aggregation time
153	  reps: number
154	  sessions: number         // distinct session count contributing
155	  avgRtMs: number | null   // correct_go RTs only; null for no-go cues
156	  best10AvgRtMs: number | null
157	  errorRate: number        // (reps - correct) / reps; defined for both go and no-go
158	  goWeakness: number | null    // for go cues only; null for no-go
159	  noGoWeakness: number | null  // for no-go cues only; null for go
160	}
161	```
162	- Eligibility: `reps ≥ 5` AND `sessions ≥ 2`. (≥5 reps alone admits "one
163	  bad session" runs; requiring 2 sessions weeds those out.)
164	- `goWeakness = (avgRtMs / 1000) + errorRate` when both are defined, else null.
165	- `noGoWeakness = errorRate` for no-go cues, else null.
166	
167	`pickTaperCues(aggregate, k)`:
168	- Splits eligible aggregates into go-pool and no-go-pool.
169	- Default split: take `ceil(k * 0.7)` from the go-pool (sorted by
170	  `goWeakness` desc, then `cueId` asc for stable tiebreak), and the rest
171	  from the no-go-pool (sorted by `noGoWeakness` desc, then `cueId` asc).
172	- If either pool is empty, fill the deficit from the other.
173	- If total eligible < k, return what we have plus a `reason` string
174	  ("Not enough data — drilled only 2 cues twice. Drill more variety first.").
175	- Returned `reason` always names the picked cues and how they were chosen
176	  (slowest go cues, highest-error no-go cues), so the UI can render a
177	  transparent banner.
178	
179	Default K = 3 with the 70/30 go/no-go split → 2 go cues + 1 no-go cue. If a
180	session is overwhelmingly one or the other, the fill-the-deficit rule
181	recovers gracefully.
182	
183	### D5a. Shared `best10AvgOf(times)` helper
184	Red-team flagged that `cueBreakdown` in `drill.ts` (lines 243-247) already
185	inlines the best-10 logic. Phase 5 would add a second copy in `analytics.ts`.
186	Three sites (cueBreakdown, sessionTrend per-session best-10, cueAggregate
187	global best-10) all encode the same invariant.
188	
189	Fix: extract `best10AvgOf(times: number[]): number | null` into
190	`engine/drill.ts` (next to summarize / cueBreakdown), export it, and
191	refactor `cueBreakdown` to call it. `analytics.ts` imports and reuses it.
192	One source of truth.
193	
194	### D6. Taper-mode profile generator
195	- New button in SettingsScreen → "Build taper profile from recent history".
196	- Modal/prompt asks for:
197	  - profile name (default `Taper — YYYY-MM-DD`)
198	  - sessions to look back (default 5)
199	  - cues to keep (default 3)
200	- Clicks "Create":
201	  - load last N sessions + their reps
202	  - compute `cueAggregate(reps)` → `pickTaperCues(agg, K)`
203	  - if recommendation is empty (not enough data): show a banner and bail
204	  - else build a profile via `buildDefaultProfile({...})` with:
205	    - `rounds: 3`
206	    - `workMs: 60_000`
207	    - `restMs: 30_000`
208	    - `maxReps: null` (round timing controls volume)
209	    - `allowedCueIds: recommendation.cueIds`
210	  - save the profile, set it active, jump back to the profile list with the
211	    new profile selected.
212	- The "low total volume" requirement is satisfied by 3×60s/30s and the cue
213	  subset (fewer cue types = fewer total reps in a fixed time at any given
214	  inter-cue tempo).
215	
216	### D7. New screen routing
217	- App has three top-level phases today: `idle | <drill phases> | ended`.
218	- Add a UI-only flag `view: 'idle' | 'analytics'` to App's local state, plus
219	  a "Analytics" link on IdleScreen next to "Settings".
220	- Analytics screen mounts when `view === 'analytics'`. Has its own back
221	  button. Does not need session-store state.
222	- Keeps store unchanged; the analytics view is pure read-from-Dexie.
223	- Loading state: "Loading sessions…" placeholder while the initial fetch
224	  is in flight (red-team called this out — IndexedDB load is async).
225	- Empty state: if zero sessions exist (or all have repCount === 0), the
226	  screen renders a CTA ("No sessions yet — run a drill first") and a
227	  back-to-idle link. No table, no compare picker.
228	
229	### D8. Session-over-session comparison view
230	- Inside AnalyticsScreen: a "Compare" mode with two `<select>` dropdowns
231	  defaulting to (second-most-recent as baseline, most-recent as candidate).
232	- Render `compareSessions(a, b, aReps, bReps)`.
233	- Top row deltas: avg RT, score, FS rate, hes rate. Color-coded by sign.
234	- `deltaScore` is suppressed (rendered as "—") when the two sessions used
235	  different `scoreWeights`, because subtracting scores computed under
236	  different rules is meaningless. The UI shows a small explanatory tooltip
237	  "Score weights differed; compare per-result rates instead."
238	- Per-cue table: red-team flagged four cases that need distinct rendering.
239	  The compare helper returns one of these classifications per cue:
240	  - `'both_measured'` — both sessions have ≥1 correct_go rep for the cue:
241	    delta-RT and delta-error-rate render normally.
242	  - `'both_error_only'` — both sessions have reps but no correct_go on at
243	    least one side: delta-RT is null, delta-error-rate renders, row is
244	    flagged red (this is the regression case red-team flagged — a cue
245	    that *was* fine and is now 100% errors must not hide behind a null).
246	  - `'candidate_only'` — cue appeared in candidate but not baseline: row
247	    annotated "new cue this session" (likely a profile change; not a
248	    regression).
249	  - `'baseline_only'` — cue appeared in baseline but not candidate: row
250	    annotated "not drilled this session" (likely a profile change; not a
251	    regression).
252	- Test fixtures cover all four classifications.
253	
254	### D9. Where new state lives
255	- Engine: `engine/analytics.ts` (new, pure).
256	- Store: `db.ts` gains `listRepsForSessions`; nothing else changes.
257	- UI: `ui/AnalyticsScreen.tsx` (new). `ui/IdleScreen.tsx` adds the link.
258	  `ui/SettingsScreen.tsx` adds the taper-builder section.
259	- Types: no breaking changes. `analytics.ts` defines its own view types.
260	  `engine/types.ts` is untouched.
261	
262	### D10. Backward compatibility
263	- Older Phase 1/2/3/4 sessions still appear in the trend view because the
264	  analytics layer reads from `RepRecord` (cueId / result / reactionMs /
265	  sessionId / cueShownAt) — every field has been populated since Phase 1.
266	- Sessions with non-default `scoreWeights` are *not* re-scored; their `score`
267	  is what the user saw at the time. The trend view shows `score` as-is.
268	  The comparison view explicitly suppresses `deltaScore` when the two
269	  sessions used different weights (see D8); the trend chart shows each
270	  session's score on its own row, no implicit comparison.
271	
272	## Risks and mitigations
273	- **Dexie `anyOf(...)` over 20 session IDs returns thousands of reps.**
274	  Mitigation: a 5-rounds × 120s session at one rep / 3s is ~200 reps; 20 such
275	  sessions is ~4000 reps. Comfortably under the IndexedDB-cursor-and-render
276	  budget. We do not paginate.
277	- **Single-rep outliers skew taper picks.** Mitigation: ≥5 reps per cue floor
278	  in `pickTaperCues`; reason string makes the basis transparent.
279	- **Most recent session may be a partial/empty session if the user opened
280	  and abandoned the app.** Mitigation: the trend view filters out sessions
281	  with `repCount === 0` for visual clarity (still queryable from compare
282	  picker if the user wants).
283	- **Taper profile generator could silently land on a profile with no go
284	  cues** if the bottom-K is all no-go cues. Mitigation: post-filter — if the
285	  picked set has no go cue, expand by one until it does, or fall back to
286	  "not enough variety, please drill more variety first" banner.
287	- **Comparison view divides by zero** when a session has zero reps of a
288	  certain cue. Mitigation: helper returns `null` for delta-RT and `0` for
289	  delta-error-rate when either side has zero reps of that cue (explicit
290	  "n/a in baseline" marker in the UI).
291	
292	## Test strategy
293	- **analytics.test.ts**: deterministic fixture reps spanning two sessions →
294	  `sessionTrend` returns expected per-session row with hand-computed FS
295	  rate, hesitation rate, avg-RT, best-10. Mixed-cue fixture →
296	  `cueTrend`, `cueAggregate` return expected rows.
297	- **compareSessions edges**: explicit fixtures for all four red-team
298	  classifications: `both_measured`, `both_error_only` (was-fine-now-100%-
299	  errors regression), `candidate_only`, `baseline_only`. Plus a fixture
300	  where the two sessions have different `scoreWeights` → `deltaScore` is
301	  null (or the helper sets a `weightsDiffer: true` flag).
302	- **pickTaperCues**: expected top-K with mixed go and no-go cues honors
303	  the 70/30 split; fallback when go-pool is empty; fallback when no-go-pool
304	  is empty; eligibility floor (drops cues with reps < 5 OR sessions < 2);
305	  ties broken by `cueId` ascending; "not enough data" reason string when
306	  total eligible < K.
307	- **best10AvgOf** unit-tested directly; `cueBreakdown` regression test
308	  confirms it still returns the same numbers after the refactor.
309	- **db.test.ts** (extend existing or add): `listRepsForSessions` round-trips
310	  reps for a known sessionId set, including the case where one of the IDs
311	  has zero reps (returns an empty array for that key, not absent).
312	- **SettingsScreen** (existing test file or new): smoke-test that clicking
313	  "Build taper profile" with mocked listRecentSessions + listRepsForSessions
314	  produces a profile with the expected `rounds`, `workMs`, `restMs`,
315	  `allowedCueIds`.
316	- **Browser**: qa-playwright runs a fresh session, then a second session,
317	  opens Analytics, verifies the trend table renders two rows; opens the
318	  compare picker, picks the two sessions, verifies the per-cue delta table
319	  renders; builds a taper profile and verifies the new profile appears in
320	  Settings with the expected reduced cue list.
321	
322	## Rollback path
323	Phase 5 lives entirely under `app/`. Reverting the phase commit restores
324	Phase 4. No Dexie schema bump → no data migration to undo. The taper-built
325	profile is just another row in the `profiles` table; users who downgrade
326	keep it but the build-button disappears.
327	
328	## Out-of-scope deferred
329	- Video clips → Phase 6
330	- Webcam pose detection → Phase 7
331	- CSV/JSON export (MVP feature 10) — still deferred; tracked separately.
332	- Cross-session anti-rhythm trend — explicitly out of Phase 5 scope.
333	- Distance-axis-aware analytics breakdown — Phase 4 stored `distance` on
334	  reps but the cross-session distance × cue matrix is deferred.

# Phase 2b decision memo — Phone-as-Sensor decomposition

(Supersedes the Phase 5 memo. Prior memos preserved in git history.)

## Decision summary

Phase 2b is decomposed into **four sub-phases**, each independently shippable
and verifiable, totaling roughly 1–2 hours of focused work per sub-phase.

| Sub-phase | Title | Ships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2b.1 | LAN companion-page hosting + manual offer/answer signaling skeleton | Phone loads a page from the laptop. Manual SDP copy-paste establishes a WebRTC DataChannel. |
| 2b.2 | QR-code pairing flow | Replace manual paste with QR scan; laptop generates QR, phone scans, answer SDP sent back via second QR or short LAN HTTP POST. |
| 2b.3 | Accelerometer threshold detection + calibration screen | Phone produces "commit" events on motion impulses. Laptop has a calibration screen that tunes per-athlete threshold. |
| 2b.4 | Wire `inputSource = 'phone'` into the drill engine + session metadata | Athlete selects "Phone" in Settings; reps stored with `inputSource: 'phone'`; analytics treats it like pedal. |

Recommended ship order is 2b.1 → 2b.2 → 2b.3 → 2b.4. The minimal next slice
(implemented in a later iteration) is **2b.1**. Everything else builds on the
transport it establishes.

The hard problems (signaling, hosting, iOS HTTPS) are answered up front so
each sub-phase has unambiguous scope.

## Options considered for the *signaling* problem

The athlete and laptop are on the same Wi-Fi. The phone must hand the laptop
its WebRTC SDP answer (and ICE candidates) somehow. Three options:

### Option A — Manual SDP copy/paste in textareas
- Laptop renders `RTCPeerConnection.createOffer()` as base64 text in a
  textarea. User copies it onto the phone (typing-too-long; only viable if
  paired with QR — see 2b.2).
- Pure P2P. No server at all.
- Pro: zero infra, fits the local-first guarantee literally.
- Con: UX is unusable as a steady state, but it's the right *scaffold* —
  prove the WebRTC path works before adding QR.

### Option B — QR code for offer, QR or short LAN HTTP POST for answer
- Laptop generates QR containing offer SDP + ICE candidates (compressed +
  base64). Phone scans, creates answer, then either:
  - **B1**: phone renders its own QR with the answer; laptop's webcam scans
    it (requires laptop webcam access + a second scan flow — heavy).
  - **B2**: phone POSTs its answer to a tiny laptop-side HTTP endpoint on
    the same origin that served the companion page. Endpoint lives in the
    same Vite dev plugin / static handler that serves the SPA. This is
    *not* a remote signaling server; it's a localhost listener bound to
    the LAN interface and dies when the laptop closes the tab/app.
  - **B3**: laptop polls a known-shape QR field on the phone screen via
    user-driven re-scan (one QR each way, user clicks "I scanned it" —
    only requires phone camera, which we already need).
- Pro: one-shot pairing the user actually wants.
- Con: needs either webcam access on laptop (B1), a laptop HTTP listener
  (B2), or asks the user to do two scans (B3).

### Option C — Tiny LAN WebSocket signaling server bundled into the app
- Run a `ws://` server on the laptop (Node, or a Vite plugin in dev /
  Tauri or Electron in prod). Phone connects via `ws://laptop-lan-ip:port`
  to swap SDP, then WebRTC peer-to-peer takes over.
- Pro: simplest signaling code path (well-known WebSocket dance), supports
  reconnect and richer pairing UX.
- Con: introduces a server process. The project today is a static SPA
  served by `vite build → dist/` with no runtime backend (per
  ARCHITECTURE.md). Adding a Node server means either (a) requiring a
  `pnpm run companion-server` step the user must keep running, or (b)
  packaging the app via Tauri/Electron. Both are bigger commitments than
  Phase 2b warrants.

### Recommendation: **Option A scaffold for 2b.1, then Option B3 (two-QR scan) for 2b.2**

- 2b.1 lands the WebRTC DataChannel with copy-paste textareas. This proves
  the transport works without committing to a signaling UX.
- 2b.2 replaces the copy-paste with QR codes on both ends. The laptop has a
  webcam already (it's where the user trains), so it can scan the phone's
  answer QR. Two scans is acceptable one-time setup; once paired, the
  DataChannel persists for the session.
- Reject Option C: a real signaling server breaks the "static SPA, no
  server" architecture. We may revisit if the user reports the two-QR
  flow is too slow in practice — at which point a Vite dev-server plugin
  that exposes a `/signal` POST endpoint is a small follow-up (Option B2
  becomes viable).

Tradeoff: Option C would give a nicer first-time flow but pulls in a
runtime dependency the project does not have. Pairing is rare (once per
training session, often once per week); two QR scans is acceptable.

## Options considered for the *companion page hosting* problem

The phone needs a URL to load. Three options:

### Option H1 — Same Vite SPA, separate route (`/phone`)
- Add a route check at the top of `App.tsx` (or before mount in
  `main.tsx`) that swaps the root component when `location.pathname`
  starts with `/phone`. Phone renders a tiny companion UI; laptop renders
  the existing trainer UI.
- Same `dist/` output. Same dev server. Same origin → no CORS, same
  cookies/localStorage if we ever needed them.
- Bundle cost: the phone pulls down the same JS that drives the laptop.
  Bundle is 341 KB / 105 KB gzip today; phone is on the same Wi-Fi; this
  is fine. Code-split the phone route only if measured to be slow.

### Option H2 — Separate static HTML file (`public/phone.html`) with its own tiny bundle
- A second Vite entry point. Phone loads `phone.html`; laptop loads
  `index.html`.
- Pro: phone bundle stays small and independent.
- Con: dual Vite entries; more build config; risk of types drift across
  two roots; doesn't share `engine/types.ts` for the wire-format
  definitions unless we still import them.

### Option H3 — Separate sub-project / sibling package
- Heavy. Overkill for two screens.

### Recommendation: **H1 (same SPA, `/phone` route)**

- Cheapest. One bundle, one source tree, shared TS types for the wire
  format. The DataChannel message shape lives in one file
  (`app/src/phone/wire.ts`) imported by both roots.
- Code-split later if the phone bundle becomes a problem.

**How does the phone discover/load it?** The laptop trainer renders a QR
code (rendered during 2b.2; manual URL during 2b.1) containing
`https://<laptop-lan-ip>:5173/phone#<offer-sdp>` (dev) or
`https://<laptop-lan-ip>:4173/phone#<offer-sdp>` (`vite preview`). The
offer SDP rides in the URL fragment so the phone gets it on first load
without a second exchange — the fragment is never sent to a server,
which is fine because there is no server.

For LAN IP discovery, prompt the user once in Settings: "Your laptop's
LAN IP (e.g. 192.168.1.42)". Persist in `SettingsRecord`. We do not
auto-detect (browsers don't expose host LAN IP). A small "Test"
button does a `fetch('/phone')` to confirm.

## Options considered for the *iOS DeviceMotion HTTPS* problem

iOS Safari blocks `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` over plain HTTP.
Android Chrome does not. Three options:

### Option I1 — mkcert-issued local CA, document setup
- User installs mkcert, generates a cert for their LAN IP, and Vite serves
  with HTTPS. Phone trusts the cert (on iOS this means installing the
  root CA profile, which is a known but real friction point).
- Pro: real HTTPS, works on iOS, works on Android, no warnings.
- Con: one-time setup is non-trivial. Documented in `docs/` not in-app.

### Option I2 — Self-signed cert + accept-warning on phone
- Cheaper to set up but every browser warns on every reconnect. iOS Safari
  *still* will not grant DeviceMotion permission for a cert it doesn't
  trust — verified behavior across iOS 15+.
- Rejected on iOS. Works in a degraded "warning every time" mode on
  Android.

### Option I3 — Defer iOS entirely; ship Android-only first
- Document that the companion page works on Android out of the box over
  HTTP (Chrome doesn't gate motion events on HTTPS), and iOS requires
  the mkcert setup in I1.
- Phase 2b.1 ships as "works on Android over HTTP." Phase 2b.3 documents
  mkcert as the path to iOS support but doesn't *require* it for
  acceptance.

### Recommendation: **I3 for 2b.1–2b.3; I1 documented for iOS users**

- We test the whole pipeline on Android in CI / qa-playwright (no iOS
  emulator in the toolchain anyway).
- `docs/SETUP_IOS.md` (new, owned by 2b.3) walks the iOS user through
  mkcert + cert install.
- 2b.3 acceptance does **not** require iOS-on-HTTP working; it requires
  Android-on-HTTP working AND an iOS user can follow the doc to enable
  motion permission. Mention both `vite --host --https` (config) and
  `vite preview --host --https` (production-build serve) in the doc.

Tradeoff: the athlete may be on iOS. If so, they do the one-time mkcert
dance once. We do not invest engineering time wrestling with iOS quirks
on the happy path.

## Recommended approach: ship order and dependency chain

```
2b.1 (transport)  →  2b.2 (QR pairing UX)  →  2b.3 (motion + calibration)  →  2b.4 (engine wiring)
```

Each later phase depends on the prior one's transport guarantee. Reasoning:

- **2b.1 first** because *nothing else can be verified* until a phone can
  open a DataChannel to the laptop. The transport is the riskiest unknown
  (WebRTC + LAN); ship it stand-alone with the worst UX (copy-paste) and
  prove it works.
- **2b.2 next** because the QR flow is purely a UX upgrade over 2b.1 — it
  swaps how SDP bytes move between the two devices but keeps the
  DataChannel logic identical. Easy to A/B against 2b.1 manually.
- **2b.3 next** because motion detection has its own calibration concerns
  (per-athlete threshold) and would muddy the waters if combined with
  transport debugging. With transport already trusted, a 2b.3 failure is
  unambiguously a sensor-side bug.
- **2b.4 last** because wiring `inputSource = 'phone'` into the existing
  drill engine is a small, mechanical change once a "commit" event
  arrives reliably. Doing it before 2b.3 would force us to fake commit
  events, which we already do in tests.

The minimal sub-phase to take first (in the *next* iteration): **2b.1**.

---

## Sub-phase 2b.1 — LAN companion-page + WebRTC DataChannel with manual SDP

### Scope
- Add `/phone` route to the existing SPA via `H1`.
- Build the WebRTC offer/answer dance on both sides.
- "Pair" screen on laptop shows offer SDP in a textarea + paste-area for
  the answer.
- Companion page on phone shows offer paste-area + answer textarea +
  "Send commit" button (manual button, not motion — that's 2b.3).
- DataChannel echoes a single `{ type: 'commit', t: number }` message on
  the button. Laptop displays "commit received at +Xms" — debug surface
  only, not yet wired to the drill.
- Settings gains a "Laptop LAN IP" field used to build the phone URL.

### Files to touch / add
- `app/src/main.tsx` — route on `location.pathname.startsWith('/phone')`
  to a new `PhoneApp` root; otherwise mount the existing `App`.
- `app/src/phone/PhoneApp.tsx` — new: phone-side root with offer paste +
  answer textarea + "Send commit" button.
- `app/src/phone/wire.ts` — new: shared TS types for the DataChannel
  messages (`PhoneEvent = { type: 'commit'; t: number } | { type:
  'calibration'; ... }`).
- `app/src/phone/peer.ts` — new: pure-ish wrapper around
  `RTCPeerConnection` + DataChannel. Symmetric API used by both ends.
- `app/src/ui/PairScreen.tsx` — new: laptop-side pairing UI launched
  from Settings or a new "Pair phone" button on IdleScreen.
- `app/src/ui/SettingsScreen.tsx` — add "Laptop LAN IP" field.
- `app/src/store/settings-types.ts` — add `laptopLanIp?: string` to
  `SettingsRecord`.
- `app/src/store/settings.ts` — pass-through for the new field in
  load/save.
- `app/index.html` — unchanged (single entry).
- `app/vite.config.ts` — add `server.host: true` (already needed to
  serve on LAN IP). Add `preview.host: true` for production-build
  serve.

### Acceptance criteria
- Loading `http://<laptop-lan-ip>:5173/phone` on a phone on the same
  Wi-Fi renders the PhoneApp.
- From the laptop's Pair screen, copying the offer to the phone, copying
  the answer back, and clicking "Connect" produces a `connected`
  DataChannel within 5 seconds.
- Pressing the phone's "Send commit" button updates a "Last commit at"
  line on the laptop Pair screen within 200ms (LAN RTT is typically
  <30ms; budget is generous).
- All 105 existing tests pass. New tests cover `wire.ts` types/encoding
  if any, and `peer.ts` with stub `RTCPeerConnection` for offer/answer
  pure logic.
- Lint + tsc + vite build clean.

### Open technical decisions
- **STUN server**: WebRTC needs at least one STUN server for ICE
  gathering even on a LAN if there's any NAT (most home Wi-Fi has no
  NAT between client and gateway → ICE host candidates suffice). Start
  with `iceServers: []` (host candidates only) and document that mesh
  networks may need `stun:stun.l.google.com:19302` as a fallback.
  Using a public STUN is a one-shot UDP packet, not ongoing traffic;
  this stays effectively local-first.
- **Base64 SDP length**: SDP blobs run 1.5–3 KB. Manual paste is
  tolerable in 2b.1; QR in 2b.2 will need a chunked QR or numeric-mode
  compression (or, simpler, gzip+base64).
- **Reconnect**: if the phone screen sleeps or the DataChannel drops,
  user re-pairs from scratch in 2b.1. Auto-reconnect is out of scope.

### Test strategy
- `app/src/phone/peer.test.ts`: stub `RTCPeerConnection` (jsdom doesn't
  provide it); verify that `createOffer → setLocalDescription →
  exposed SDP string` flows. Mostly tests our wrapper, not WebRTC.
- `app/src/phone/wire.test.ts`: type-narrowing tests for the message
  union, JSON round-trip on each message variant.
- Manual qa-playwright: open laptop in one browser context, phone-sized
  context on `/phone`, paste offer/answer between them, click commit,
  assert the laptop screen updates. (No real WebRTC under Playwright
  because jsdom and headless contexts don't fully implement it — this
  may need to be a real-browser Playwright run, not headless. Document
  this in QA notes.)
- Manual real-device: laptop + phone on same Wi-Fi, paste flow works.
  Logged as a "Phase 2b.1 manual QA checklist" in the verify artifact.

### Risks and mitigations
- *WebRTC under headless Playwright is flaky*: drop to logic-level tests
  in vitest; mark the end-to-end pairing as a documented manual step in
  the verify artifact. (Phase 4 already has a `verify-phase4.mjs`
  manual script; same pattern.)
- *Same-origin policy + mixed content*: if Phase 2b.3 introduces HTTPS,
  this works because Vite dev-server with `--host --https` covers
  both. 2b.1 sticks to HTTP for Android-only; iOS users will see
  acceptance fail at 2b.3 without mkcert (documented).
- *Bundle bloat from including `RTCPeerConnection` polyfill*: none —
  it's a native browser API.

### Rollback path
The entire `phone/` subtree is new code; the `/phone` route is
isolated. Removing the route guard in `main.tsx` and dropping the
`phone/` directory reverts cleanly. `SettingsRecord.laptopLanIp` is
optional → not a schema migration.

---

## Sub-phase 2b.2 — QR-code pairing flow

### Scope
- Replace the textarea copy-paste in 2b.1 with two QR exchanges:
  1. Laptop renders a QR containing the URL + offer SDP (gzipped +
     base64 in the URL fragment).
  2. Phone scans, opens the URL, auto-applies the offer, computes the
     answer, then renders its own QR with the compressed answer SDP.
  3. Laptop uses `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true })`
     + a tiny in-browser QR decoder to read the phone's answer QR.
- "Pair" screen on laptop has three states: showing-offer, scanning-
  answer, connected.

### Files to touch / add
- `app/src/phone/qr.ts` — new: QR encode (offer) + QR decode (answer)
  helpers. Vendor a small dependency: `jsqr` (decode, ~40 KB) +
  `qrcode` (encode, ~30 KB) — both pure-JS, tree-shakeable. Add to
  `package.json`.
- `app/src/ui/PairScreen.tsx` — extend the 2b.1 UI: add QR display
  for offer, webcam preview + jsqr scan loop for answer.
- `app/src/phone/PhoneApp.tsx` — auto-parse offer from URL fragment;
  render answer QR.

### Acceptance criteria
- User clicks "Pair phone" on laptop → QR appears.
- User scans QR with phone camera → PhoneApp loads, auto-applies offer,
  renders an answer QR within 3 seconds.
- User points laptop webcam at phone screen → laptop auto-detects QR
  and establishes DataChannel within 5 seconds total.
- Manual textarea path from 2b.1 remains available behind a "Show
  manual pairing" toggle (fallback for environments without a laptop
  webcam).
- All tests still pass; lint/tsc/build clean.

### Open technical decisions
- **QR payload size**: SDP can exceed standard QR capacity. Either gzip
  before base64 (typical 30–50% reduction; usually fits in a single QR
  at error-correction level L), or chunk into multiple QRs the phone
  cycles through (more complex, last resort). Start with gzip; chunk
  only if measured to fail.
- **Webcam permission UX**: laptop needs `getUserMedia`. Prompt once,
  remember dismissal in settings. Provide a fallback toggle.
- **jsqr scan loop**: ~30 fps decode is overkill; run at 10 fps to
  keep CPU usage low.

### Test strategy
- `qr.test.ts`: round-trip a sample SDP through encode/decode at
  multiple sizes; assert chunking kicks in if (and only if) size
  exceeds threshold.
- Manual qa-playwright: cannot exercise `getUserMedia` easily;
  document as manual real-device test, same as 2b.1.
- Real-device QA: scan QR with phone, scan QR back with laptop,
  DataChannel connects.

### Risks and mitigations
- *Adding `jsqr` and `qrcode` bumps bundle ~70 KB*. Acceptable —
  current bundle is 341 KB / 105 KB gzip, and these modules can be
  lazy-loaded only when PairScreen mounts (`React.lazy` boundary
  around it).
- *Camera quality* on low-end laptops may fail to decode. The manual
  textarea path stays as fallback.

### Rollback
Hide the QR UI behind a feature flag; the manual paste from 2b.1
still works. Removing the QR helpers and reverting PairScreen to its
2b.1 shape reverts cleanly.

---

## Sub-phase 2b.3 — Accelerometer threshold detection + calibration

### Scope
- PhoneApp listens to `devicemotion` events, computes a simple impulse
  metric (jerk = derivative of acceleration magnitude, or peak
  acceleration above gravity in a sliding window), and emits a
  `{ type: 'commit', t: number }` message when the metric exceeds the
  athlete's calibrated threshold.
- New laptop-side "Calibrate" screen reachable from PairScreen and
  Settings:
  - Laptop instructs athlete to throw 5 sample punches/steps
  - Phone streams a live `{ type: 'sample', peakG: number, t: number }`
    feed for ~10 seconds
  - Laptop computes p10 of peak G values across the samples, sets
    threshold at `p10 - epsilon` to admit the athlete's softest
    intended commit. Persists per-athlete in a new `calibrations`
    Dexie store (or a field on the active profile — see open decision).
- iOS only: phone shows a "Tap to enable motion" button that calls
  `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` on user gesture.

### Files to touch / add
- `app/src/phone/motion.ts` — new: motion event listener + impulse
  metric computation. Pure function for the metric to keep it testable.
- `app/src/phone/PhoneApp.tsx` — wire up motion listener; gate behind
  a permission button on iOS; send `commit` events over DataChannel.
- `app/src/ui/CalibrateScreen.tsx` — new: laptop-side calibration UI.
- `app/src/engine/types.ts` — add `phoneCalibration?: { thresholdG:
  number; calibratedAt: number }` to `ProfileRecord.config` (or to
  SettingsRecord — see decision).
- `docs/SETUP_IOS.md` — new: mkcert walkthrough.

### Acceptance criteria
- Phone on a coffee table at rest emits **zero** commit events for 60
  seconds.
- Phone strapped to wrist or held: a sharp forward-snap motion emits
  exactly one commit event within 50ms of the impulse peak.
- Calibration screen captures 5 samples and persists the threshold;
  re-running calibration overwrites the prior value.
- Android: works over HTTP without prompts (Chrome doesn't gate
  `devicemotion`).
- iOS: with mkcert HTTPS, "Tap to enable motion" grants permission
  and commits flow.
- Documented in `docs/SETUP_IOS.md`; iOS acceptance is doc-driven, not
  CI-driven.

### Open technical decisions
- **Per-profile vs per-settings threshold**: a single athlete has one
  body; settings-singleton is simpler. But the "per-athlete" wording
  in `docs/PHASES.md` suggests profile-level. **Recommend
  per-profile** — the user already has multi-profile (Phase 4), so
  this composes. Profiles that don't have a calibration fall back to
  a sensible default (e.g. `thresholdG: 1.8` — a moderate impulse).
- **Impulse metric**: simplest is `max(|a| - g)` over a 200ms sliding
  window. More sophisticated is to compute jerk (numeric derivative)
  and threshold *that*. Start simple; revise if false-positives are
  too frequent in real-device QA.
- **Debounce**: once a commit fires, ignore further events for 300ms
  to avoid double-trigger from the recoil.

### Test strategy
- `motion.test.ts`: pure-function tests on the impulse metric and
  threshold-crossing logic. Feed synthesized accel streams (still
  baseline, one impulse, double-tap, calibration sequence) and
  assert expected commit timestamps.
- Calibration math: feed 5 sample peakG values, assert resulting
  threshold matches `p10 - epsilon`.
- qa-playwright: cannot generate fake `devicemotion` easily — mark as
  manual real-device step.
- Real-device QA: documented script in verify-phase-2b.mjs (analogous
  to verify-phase4.mjs):
  1. Connect phone.
  2. Set phone on table → no commits in 30s.
  3. Punch motion × 5 → exactly 5 commits.
  4. Run calibration → threshold persists across reload.

### Risks and mitigations
- *iOS user can't get mkcert working*: the doc is detailed; if they
  give up they can still use keyboard/pedal. Phone-as-sensor is
  marked as an optional input source in the spec.
- *Motion thresholds vary wildly by phone hardware*: the per-profile
  calibration captures this; the default is a fallback, not a claim.
- *Multiple commits per intended punch*: the 300ms debounce + jerk-
  rather-than-peak metric should mitigate. Tunable from Settings.

### Rollback
The motion code is gated behind the phone input source. Reverting to
the 2b.2 shape leaves the "Send commit" button as a manual fallback;
calibration screen is hidden.

---

## Sub-phase 2b.4 — Wire `inputSource = 'phone'` into engine + session metadata

### Scope
- Add `'phone'` to the `InputSource` union (`app/src/engine/types.ts:44`).
- Settings UI: add `<option value="phone">Phone (motion)</option>` to
  the input-source select.
- IdleScreen: if `inputSource === 'phone'` and no DataChannel is
  connected, show a banner "Phone not paired — pair now" with a button.
  Disable Start if not paired.
- TrainerScreen: subscribe to the DataChannel; on receiving a
  `commit` message, call the same `recordPress(at)` function that
  keyboard/pedal already use.
- SummaryScreen: already shows `inputSource` — no change needed.
- Analytics (Phase 5): no change; `inputSource` is opaque to it.

### Files to touch
- `app/src/engine/types.ts` — `InputSource = 'keyboard' | 'pedal' |
  'phone'`. Existing rep records remain compatible (the field is just
  a string).
- `app/src/store/session.ts` — `start()`'s `inputSource` arg already
  accepts the new value.
- `app/src/ui/SettingsScreen.tsx` — extend select options.
- `app/src/ui/IdleScreen.tsx` — pre-flight check for paired phone.
- `app/src/ui/TrainerScreen.tsx` — DataChannel subscription.
- `app/src/phone/peer.ts` — expose a singleton connection getter
  (`getPhonePeer()`) so multiple screens can subscribe.

### Acceptance criteria
- User in Settings picks "Phone", lands on Idle.
- If unpaired: banner + pair button block Start.
- If paired: Start enabled, drill runs, phone commits drive reps.
- Saved `SessionRecord.inputSource === 'phone'`.
- All 105+ existing tests still pass. New tests cover the union-
  member addition and the IdleScreen pre-flight gate.

### Open technical decisions
- **Where does the singleton peer live?** Either Zustand store or a
  module-level singleton in `phone/peer.ts`. Recommend
  module-singleton with a small React hook (`usePhonePeer()`) for
  components; mirrors how `getDb()` works today.
- **What happens if the DataChannel drops mid-session?** Pause the
  drill, banner "Phone disconnected — reconnect to continue", same
  as a pedal unplug would feel.
- **Backward compat for old `SessionRecord.inputSource`**: existing
  rows have `'keyboard' | 'pedal'`; the type widening to include
  `'phone'` is purely additive. No migration.

### Test strategy
- `session.test.ts`: extend the existing inputSource test to cover
  `'phone'`.
- `SettingsScreen` test: select "phone", verify settings persist.
- `IdleScreen` test: when inputSource is 'phone' and `getPhonePeer()`
  returns disconnected, Start is disabled.
- qa-playwright: full pair → calibrate → drill → summary flow.
  Acknowledge real-device dependency in the verify artifact.

### Rollback
The `'phone'` literal is removed from the `InputSource` union;
existing rows with `inputSource: 'phone'` would type-error on read.
Mitigation: keep the type as `'keyboard' | 'pedal' | 'phone' |
string` for one version if we ever roll back, or use a string cast
at the read boundary. Realistically, Phase 2b lands together or
not at all.

---

## Risks and mitigations (cross-cutting)

- **WebRTC is harder to test than HTTP.** Mitigation: keep transport
  logic in pure-ish modules (`peer.ts`, `wire.ts`, `motion.ts`) that
  vitest can exercise; reserve full pairing for manual real-device
  QA documented in `verify-phase-2b*.mjs`.
- **iOS HTTPS friction.** Mitigation: ship Android-only acceptance;
  doc-driven iOS support; do not block Phase 2b on iOS.
- **Bundle bloat from QR libraries.** Mitigation: `React.lazy` around
  PairScreen so the pairing modules only download when needed.
- **The phone goes to sleep mid-drill.** Mitigation: PhoneApp requests
  `screen.wakeLock` while a DataChannel is open. Falls back gracefully
  on browsers without the API (Safari < 16.4).
- **A red-team flag: a remote attacker on the same Wi-Fi could connect
  to the laptop's `/phone` endpoint and inject spurious commits.**
  Mitigation: the QR-distributed offer SDP carries a per-session
  random nonce; the laptop only accepts a DataChannel whose answer
  references that nonce. This is light auth, not a security boundary —
  the threat model is "annoyance," not "attacker on hostile network."
- **Phase 5 analytics breakage:** `inputSource = 'phone'` may surface
  in trend rows. Verify the analytics text labels handle the new value
  (probably already do; the field is opaque to most analytics math).

## Test strategy summary

Per sub-phase the unit/vitest layer covers all pure logic (wire format,
QR encode/decode, peer wrapper, motion impulse detection, calibration
math, IdleScreen gate). The manual real-device layer covers the
end-to-end pairing and motion-trigger paths; each sub-phase ships a
verify script + manual QA checklist (mirroring `verify-phase4.mjs`).

qa-playwright tests cover everything *except* WebRTC handshake and
`devicemotion` (browsers under test don't provide either reliably).
These are documented as a known limitation in the verify artifact.

## Acceptance criteria for the next implementation step (2b.1)

- New `/phone` route exists; visiting it on a phone on the same Wi-Fi
  renders `PhoneApp`.
- Laptop "Pair phone" screen produces an offer SDP textarea.
- Manual copy/paste of offer onto phone + answer onto laptop establishes
  a DataChannel within 5 seconds (in a real-device QA run).
- Pressing the phone's "Send commit" button echoes a `commit` message
  the laptop displays with a timestamp.
- `SettingsRecord` carries a new optional `laptopLanIp` field.
- All 105 existing tests pass. New unit tests for `wire.ts` and
  `peer.ts` (the parts that don't need real `RTCPeerConnection`).
- Lint + tsc + vite build clean; bundle growth budget +20 KB gzip.
- Documented manual QA steps in `app/verify-phase-2b1.mjs` (new).
- `docs/PHASES.md` updated to add 2b.1–2b.4 (a separate, builder-
  driven edit — this memo is the input).

## Out-of-scope (explicitly deferred past 2b.4)

- Multi-phone support (one phone per laptop, one DataChannel at a time).
- Phone-driven UI for selecting drills (the spec marks phone as sensor
  only, not primary UI).
- Auto-reconnect on transient drops (manual re-pair only).
- iOS-on-HTTP support (requires Apple to change Safari).
- Cloud signaling fallback (would break local-first guarantee).
- Pose-based commit detection (Phase 7).

1	# Phase 2b decision memo — Phone-as-Sensor decomposition
2	
3	(Supersedes the Phase 5 memo. Prior memos preserved in git history.)
4	
5	## Decision summary
6	
7	Phase 2b is decomposed into **four sub-phases**, each independently shippable
8	and verifiable, totaling roughly 1–2 hours of focused work per sub-phase.
9	
10	| Sub-phase | Title | Ships |
11	| --- | --- | --- |
12	| 2b.1 | LAN companion-page hosting + manual offer/answer signaling skeleton | Phone loads a page from the laptop. Manual SDP copy-paste establishes a WebRTC DataChannel. |
13	| 2b.2 | QR-code pairing flow | Replace manual paste with QR scan; laptop generates QR, phone scans, answer SDP sent back via second QR or short LAN HTTP POST. |
14	| 2b.3 | Accelerometer threshold detection + calibration screen | Phone produces "commit" events on motion impulses. Laptop has a calibration screen that tunes per-athlete threshold. |
15	| 2b.4 | Wire `inputSource = 'phone'` into the drill engine + session metadata | Athlete selects "Phone" in Settings; reps stored with `inputSource: 'phone'`; analytics treats it like pedal. |
16	
17	Recommended ship order is 2b.1 → 2b.2 → 2b.3 → 2b.4. The minimal next slice
18	(implemented in a later iteration) is **2b.1**. Everything else builds on the
19	transport it establishes.
20	
21	The hard problems (signaling, hosting, iOS HTTPS) are answered up front so
22	each sub-phase has unambiguous scope.
23	
24	## Options considered for the *signaling* problem
25	
26	The athlete and laptop are on the same Wi-Fi. The phone must hand the laptop
27	its WebRTC SDP answer (and ICE candidates) somehow. Three options:
28	
29	### Option A — Manual SDP copy/paste in textareas
30	- Laptop renders `RTCPeerConnection.createOffer()` as base64 text in a
31	  textarea. User copies it onto the phone (typing-too-long; only viable if
32	  paired with QR — see 2b.2).
33	- Pure P2P. No server at all.
34	- Pro: zero infra, fits the local-first guarantee literally.
35	- Con: UX is unusable as a steady state, but it's the right *scaffold* —
36	  prove the WebRTC path works before adding QR.
37	
38	### Option B — QR code for offer, QR or short LAN HTTP POST for answer
39	- Laptop generates QR containing offer SDP + ICE candidates (compressed +
40	  base64). Phone scans, creates answer, then either:
41	  - **B1**: phone renders its own QR with the answer; laptop's webcam scans
42	    it (requires laptop webcam access + a second scan flow — heavy).
43	  - **B2**: phone POSTs its answer to a tiny laptop-side HTTP endpoint on
44	    the same origin that served the companion page. Endpoint lives in the
45	    same Vite dev plugin / static handler that serves the SPA. This is
46	    *not* a remote signaling server; it's a localhost listener bound to
47	    the LAN interface and dies when the laptop closes the tab/app.
48	  - **B3**: laptop polls a known-shape QR field on the phone screen via
49	    user-driven re-scan (one QR each way, user clicks "I scanned it" —
50	    only requires phone camera, which we already need).
51	- Pro: one-shot pairing the user actually wants.
52	- Con: needs either webcam access on laptop (B1), a laptop HTTP listener
53	  (B2), or asks the user to do two scans (B3).
54	
55	### Option C — Tiny LAN WebSocket signaling server bundled into the app
56	- Run a `ws://` server on the laptop (Node, or a Vite plugin in dev /
57	  Tauri or Electron in prod). Phone connects via `ws://laptop-lan-ip:port`
58	  to swap SDP, then WebRTC peer-to-peer takes over.
59	- Pro: simplest signaling code path (well-known WebSocket dance), supports
60	  reconnect and richer pairing UX.
61	- Con: introduces a server process. The project today is a static SPA
62	  served by `vite build → dist/` with no runtime backend (per
63	  ARCHITECTURE.md). Adding a Node server means either (a) requiring a
64	  `pnpm run companion-server` step the user must keep running, or (b)
65	  packaging the app via Tauri/Electron. Both are bigger commitments than
66	  Phase 2b warrants.
67	
68	### Recommendation: **Option A scaffold for 2b.1, then Option B3 (two-QR scan) for 2b.2**
69	
70	- 2b.1 lands the WebRTC DataChannel with copy-paste textareas. This proves
71	  the transport works without committing to a signaling UX.
72	- 2b.2 replaces the copy-paste with QR codes on both ends. The laptop has a
73	  webcam already (it's where the user trains), so it can scan the phone's
74	  answer QR. Two scans is acceptable one-time setup; once paired, the
75	  DataChannel persists for the session.
76	- Reject Option C: a real signaling server breaks the "static SPA, no
77	  server" architecture. We may revisit if the user reports the two-QR
78	  flow is too slow in practice — at which point a Vite dev-server plugin
79	  that exposes a `/signal` POST endpoint is a small follow-up (Option B2
80	  becomes viable).
81	
82	Tradeoff: Option C would give a nicer first-time flow but pulls in a
83	runtime dependency the project does not have. Pairing is rare (once per
84	training session, often once per week); two QR scans is acceptable.
85	
86	## Options considered for the *companion page hosting* problem
87	
88	The phone needs a URL to load. Three options:
89	
90	### Option H1 — Same Vite SPA, separate route (`/phone`)
91	- Add a route check at the top of `App.tsx` (or before mount in
92	  `main.tsx`) that swaps the root component when `location.pathname`
93	  starts with `/phone`. Phone renders a tiny companion UI; laptop renders
94	  the existing trainer UI.
95	- Same `dist/` output. Same dev server. Same origin → no CORS, same
96	  cookies/localStorage if we ever needed them.
97	- Bundle cost: the phone pulls down the same JS that drives the laptop.
98	  Bundle is 341 KB / 105 KB gzip today; phone is on the same Wi-Fi; this
99	  is fine. Code-split the phone route only if measured to be slow.
100	
101	### Option H2 — Separate static HTML file (`public/phone.html`) with its own tiny bundle
102	- A second Vite entry point. Phone loads `phone.html`; laptop loads
103	  `index.html`.
104	- Pro: phone bundle stays small and independent.
105	- Con: dual Vite entries; more build config; risk of types drift across
106	  two roots; doesn't share `engine/types.ts` for the wire-format
107	  definitions unless we still import them.
108	
109	### Option H3 — Separate sub-project / sibling package
110	- Heavy. Overkill for two screens.
111	
112	### Recommendation: **H1 (same SPA, `/phone` route)**
113	
114	- Cheapest. One bundle, one source tree, shared TS types for the wire
115	  format. The DataChannel message shape lives in one file
116	  (`app/src/phone/wire.ts`) imported by both roots.
117	- Code-split later if the phone bundle becomes a problem.
118	
119	**How does the phone discover/load it?** The laptop trainer renders a QR
120	code (rendered during 2b.2; manual URL during 2b.1) containing
121	`https://<laptop-lan-ip>:5173/phone#<offer-sdp>` (dev) or
122	`https://<laptop-lan-ip>:4173/phone#<offer-sdp>` (`vite preview`). The
123	offer SDP rides in the URL fragment so the phone gets it on first load
124	without a second exchange — the fragment is never sent to a server,
125	which is fine because there is no server.
126	
127	For LAN IP discovery, prompt the user once in Settings: "Your laptop's
128	LAN IP (e.g. 192.168.1.42)". Persist in `SettingsRecord`. We do not
129	auto-detect (browsers don't expose host LAN IP). A small "Test"
130	button does a `fetch('/phone')` to confirm.
131	
132	## Options considered for the *iOS DeviceMotion HTTPS* problem
133	
134	iOS Safari blocks `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` over plain HTTP.
135	Android Chrome does not. Three options:
136	
137	### Option I1 — mkcert-issued local CA, document setup
138	- User installs mkcert, generates a cert for their LAN IP, and Vite serves
139	  with HTTPS. Phone trusts the cert (on iOS this means installing the
140	  root CA profile, which is a known but real friction point).
141	- Pro: real HTTPS, works on iOS, works on Android, no warnings.
142	- Con: one-time setup is non-trivial. Documented in `docs/` not in-app.
143	
144	### Option I2 — Self-signed cert + accept-warning on phone
145	- Cheaper to set up but every browser warns on every reconnect. iOS Safari
146	  *still* will not grant DeviceMotion permission for a cert it doesn't
147	  trust — verified behavior across iOS 15+.
148	- Rejected on iOS. Works in a degraded "warning every time" mode on
149	  Android.
150	
151	### Option I3 — Defer iOS entirely; ship Android-only first
152	- Document that the companion page works on Android out of the box over
153	  HTTP (Chrome doesn't gate motion events on HTTPS), and iOS requires
154	  the mkcert setup in I1.
155	- Phase 2b.1 ships as "works on Android over HTTP." Phase 2b.3 documents
156	  mkcert as the path to iOS support but doesn't *require* it for
157	  acceptance.
158	
159	### Recommendation: **I3 for 2b.1–2b.3; I1 documented for iOS users**
160	
161	- We test the whole pipeline on Android in CI / qa-playwright (no iOS
162	  emulator in the toolchain anyway).
163	- `docs/SETUP_IOS.md` (new, owned by 2b.3) walks the iOS user through
164	  mkcert + cert install.
165	- 2b.3 acceptance does **not** require iOS-on-HTTP working; it requires
166	  Android-on-HTTP working AND an iOS user can follow the doc to enable
167	  motion permission. Mention both `vite --host --https` (config) and
168	  `vite preview --host --https` (production-build serve) in the doc.
169	
170	Tradeoff: the athlete may be on iOS. If so, they do the one-time mkcert
171	dance once. We do not invest engineering time wrestling with iOS quirks
172	on the happy path.
173	
174	## Recommended approach: ship order and dependency chain
175	
176	```
177	2b.1 (transport)  →  2b.2 (QR pairing UX)  →  2b.3 (motion + calibration)  →  2b.4 (engine wiring)
178	```
179	
180	Each later phase depends on the prior one's transport guarantee. Reasoning:
181	
182	- **2b.1 first** because *nothing else can be verified* until a phone can
183	  open a DataChannel to the laptop. The transport is the riskiest unknown
184	  (WebRTC + LAN); ship it stand-alone with the worst UX (copy-paste) and
185	  prove it works.
186	- **2b.2 next** because the QR flow is purely a UX upgrade over 2b.1 — it
187	  swaps how SDP bytes move between the two devices but keeps the
188	  DataChannel logic identical. Easy to A/B against 2b.1 manually.
189	- **2b.3 next** because motion detection has its own calibration concerns
190	  (per-athlete threshold) and would muddy the waters if combined with
191	  transport debugging. With transport already trusted, a 2b.3 failure is
192	  unambiguously a sensor-side bug.
193	- **2b.4 last** because wiring `inputSource = 'phone'` into the existing
194	  drill engine is a small, mechanical change once a "commit" event
195	  arrives reliably. Doing it before 2b.3 would force us to fake commit
196	  events, which we already do in tests.
197	
198	The minimal sub-phase to take first (in the *next* iteration): **2b.1**.
199	
200	---
201	
202	## Sub-phase 2b.1 — LAN companion-page + WebRTC DataChannel with manual SDP
203	
204	### Scope
205	- Add `/phone` route to the existing SPA via `H1`.
206	- Build the WebRTC offer/answer dance on both sides.
207	- "Pair" screen on laptop shows offer SDP in a textarea + paste-area for
208	  the answer.
209	- Companion page on phone shows offer paste-area + answer textarea +
210	  "Send commit" button (manual button, not motion — that's 2b.3).
211	- DataChannel echoes a single `{ type: 'commit', t: number }` message on
212	  the button. Laptop displays "commit received at +Xms" — debug surface
213	  only, not yet wired to the drill.
214	- Settings gains a "Laptop LAN IP" field used to build the phone URL.
215	
216	### Files to touch / add
217	- `app/src/main.tsx` — route on `location.pathname.startsWith('/phone')`
218	  to a new `PhoneApp` root; otherwise mount the existing `App`.
219	- `app/src/phone/PhoneApp.tsx` — new: phone-side root with offer paste +
220	  answer textarea + "Send commit" button.
221	- `app/src/phone/wire.ts` — new: shared TS types for the DataChannel
222	  messages (`PhoneEvent = { type: 'commit'; t: number } | { type:
223	  'calibration'; ... }`).
224	- `app/src/phone/peer.ts` — new: pure-ish wrapper around
225	  `RTCPeerConnection` + DataChannel. Symmetric API used by both ends.
226	- `app/src/ui/PairScreen.tsx` — new: laptop-side pairing UI launched
227	  from Settings or a new "Pair phone" button on IdleScreen.
228	- `app/src/ui/SettingsScreen.tsx` — add "Laptop LAN IP" field.
229	- `app/src/store/settings-types.ts` — add `laptopLanIp?: string` to
230	  `SettingsRecord`.
231	- `app/src/store/settings.ts` — pass-through for the new field in
232	  load/save.
233	- `app/index.html` — unchanged (single entry).
234	- `app/vite.config.ts` — add `server.host: true` (already needed to
235	  serve on LAN IP). Add `preview.host: true` for production-build
236	  serve.
237	
238	### Acceptance criteria
239	- Loading `http://<laptop-lan-ip>:5173/phone` on a phone on the same
240	  Wi-Fi renders the PhoneApp.
241	- From the laptop's Pair screen, copying the offer to the phone, copying
242	  the answer back, and clicking "Connect" produces a `connected`
243	  DataChannel within 5 seconds.
244	- Pressing the phone's "Send commit" button updates a "Last commit at"
245	  line on the laptop Pair screen within 200ms (LAN RTT is typically
246	  <30ms; budget is generous).
247	- All 105 existing tests pass. New tests cover `wire.ts` types/encoding
248	  if any, and `peer.ts` with stub `RTCPeerConnection` for offer/answer
249	  pure logic.
250	- Lint + tsc + vite build clean.
251	
252	### Open technical decisions
253	- **STUN server**: WebRTC needs at least one STUN server for ICE
254	  gathering even on a LAN if there's any NAT (most home Wi-Fi has no
255	  NAT between client and gateway → ICE host candidates suffice). Start
256	  with `iceServers: []` (host candidates only) and document that mesh
257	  networks may need `stun:stun.l.google.com:19302` as a fallback.
258	  Using a public STUN is a one-shot UDP packet, not ongoing traffic;
259	  this stays effectively local-first.
260	- **Base64 SDP length**: SDP blobs run 1.5–3 KB. Manual paste is
261	  tolerable in 2b.1; QR in 2b.2 will need a chunked QR or numeric-mode
262	  compression (or, simpler, gzip+base64).
263	- **Reconnect**: if the phone screen sleeps or the DataChannel drops,
264	  user re-pairs from scratch in 2b.1. Auto-reconnect is out of scope.
265	
266	### Test strategy
267	- `app/src/phone/peer.test.ts`: stub `RTCPeerConnection` (jsdom doesn't
268	  provide it); verify that `createOffer → setLocalDescription →
269	  exposed SDP string` flows. Mostly tests our wrapper, not WebRTC.
270	- `app/src/phone/wire.test.ts`: type-narrowing tests for the message
271	  union, JSON round-trip on each message variant.
272	- Manual qa-playwright: open laptop in one browser context, phone-sized
273	  context on `/phone`, paste offer/answer between them, click commit,
274	  assert the laptop screen updates. (No real WebRTC under Playwright
275	  because jsdom and headless contexts don't fully implement it — this
276	  may need to be a real-browser Playwright run, not headless. Document
277	  this in QA notes.)
278	- Manual real-device: laptop + phone on same Wi-Fi, paste flow works.
279	  Logged as a "Phase 2b.1 manual QA checklist" in the verify artifact.
280	
281	### Risks and mitigations
282	- *WebRTC under headless Playwright is flaky*: drop to logic-level tests
283	  in vitest; mark the end-to-end pairing as a documented manual step in
284	  the verify artifact. (Phase 4 already has a `verify-phase4.mjs`
285	  manual script; same pattern.)
286	- *Same-origin policy + mixed content*: if Phase 2b.3 introduces HTTPS,
287	  this works because Vite dev-server with `--host --https` covers
288	  both. 2b.1 sticks to HTTP for Android-only; iOS users will see
289	  acceptance fail at 2b.3 without mkcert (documented).
290	- *Bundle bloat from including `RTCPeerConnection` polyfill*: none —
291	  it's a native browser API.
292	
293	### Rollback path
294	The entire `phone/` subtree is new code; the `/phone` route is
295	isolated. Removing the route guard in `main.tsx` and dropping the
296	`phone/` directory reverts cleanly. `SettingsRecord.laptopLanIp` is
297	optional → not a schema migration.
298	
299	---
300	
301	## Sub-phase 2b.2 — QR-code pairing flow
302	
303	### Scope
304	- Replace the textarea copy-paste in 2b.1 with two QR exchanges:
305	  1. Laptop renders a QR containing the URL + offer SDP (gzipped +
306	     base64 in the URL fragment).
307	  2. Phone scans, opens the URL, auto-applies the offer, computes the
308	     answer, then renders its own QR with the compressed answer SDP.
309	  3. Laptop uses `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true })`
310	     + a tiny in-browser QR decoder to read the phone's answer QR.
311	- "Pair" screen on laptop has three states: showing-offer, scanning-
312	  answer, connected.
313	
314	### Files to touch / add
315	- `app/src/phone/qr.ts` — new: QR encode (offer) + QR decode (answer)
316	  helpers. Vendor a small dependency: `jsqr` (decode, ~40 KB) +
317	  `qrcode` (encode, ~30 KB) — both pure-JS, tree-shakeable. Add to
318	  `package.json`.
319	- `app/src/ui/PairScreen.tsx` — extend the 2b.1 UI: add QR display
320	  for offer, webcam preview + jsqr scan loop for answer.
321	- `app/src/phone/PhoneApp.tsx` — auto-parse offer from URL fragment;
322	  render answer QR.
323	
324	### Acceptance criteria
325	- User clicks "Pair phone" on laptop → QR appears.
326	- User scans QR with phone camera → PhoneApp loads, auto-applies offer,
327	  renders an answer QR within 3 seconds.
328	- User points laptop webcam at phone screen → laptop auto-detects QR
329	  and establishes DataChannel within 5 seconds total.
330	- Manual textarea path from 2b.1 remains available behind a "Show
331	  manual pairing" toggle (fallback for environments without a laptop
332	  webcam).
333	- All tests still pass; lint/tsc/build clean.
334	
335	### Open technical decisions
336	- **QR payload size**: SDP can exceed standard QR capacity. Either gzip
337	  before base64 (typical 30–50% reduction; usually fits in a single QR
338	  at error-correction level L), or chunk into multiple QRs the phone
339	  cycles through (more complex, last resort). Start with gzip; chunk
340	  only if measured to fail.
341	- **Webcam permission UX**: laptop needs `getUserMedia`. Prompt once,
342	  remember dismissal in settings. Provide a fallback toggle.
343	- **jsqr scan loop**: ~30 fps decode is overkill; run at 10 fps to
344	  keep CPU usage low.
345	
346	### Test strategy
347	- `qr.test.ts`: round-trip a sample SDP through encode/decode at
348	  multiple sizes; assert chunking kicks in if (and only if) size
349	  exceeds threshold.
350	- Manual qa-playwright: cannot exercise `getUserMedia` easily;
351	  document as manual real-device test, same as 2b.1.
352	- Real-device QA: scan QR with phone, scan QR back with laptop,
353	  DataChannel connects.
354	
355	### Risks and mitigations
356	- *Adding `jsqr` and `qrcode` bumps bundle ~70 KB*. Acceptable —
357	  current bundle is 341 KB / 105 KB gzip, and these modules can be
358	  lazy-loaded only when PairScreen mounts (`React.lazy` boundary
359	  around it).
360	- *Camera quality* on low-end laptops may fail to decode. The manual
361	  textarea path stays as fallback.
362	
363	### Rollback
364	Hide the QR UI behind a feature flag; the manual paste from 2b.1
365	still works. Removing the QR helpers and reverting PairScreen to its
366	2b.1 shape reverts cleanly.
367	
368	---
369	
370	## Sub-phase 2b.3 — Accelerometer threshold detection + calibration
371	
372	### Scope
373	- PhoneApp listens to `devicemotion` events, computes a simple impulse
374	  metric (jerk = derivative of acceleration magnitude, or peak
375	  acceleration above gravity in a sliding window), and emits a
376	  `{ type: 'commit', t: number }` message when the metric exceeds the
377	  athlete's calibrated threshold.
378	- New laptop-side "Calibrate" screen reachable from PairScreen and
379	  Settings:
380	  - Laptop instructs athlete to throw 5 sample punches/steps
381	  - Phone streams a live `{ type: 'sample', peakG: number, t: number }`
382	    feed for ~10 seconds
383	  - Laptop computes p10 of peak G values across the samples, sets
384	    threshold at `p10 - epsilon` to admit the athlete's softest
385	    intended commit. Persists per-athlete in a new `calibrations`
386	    Dexie store (or a field on the active profile — see open decision).
387	- iOS only: phone shows a "Tap to enable motion" button that calls
388	  `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` on user gesture.
389	
390	### Files to touch / add
391	- `app/src/phone/motion.ts` — new: motion event listener + impulse
392	  metric computation. Pure function for the metric to keep it testable.
393	- `app/src/phone/PhoneApp.tsx` — wire up motion listener; gate behind
394	  a permission button on iOS; send `commit` events over DataChannel.
395	- `app/src/ui/CalibrateScreen.tsx` — new: laptop-side calibration UI.
396	- `app/src/engine/types.ts` — add `phoneCalibration?: { thresholdG:
397	  number; calibratedAt: number }` to `ProfileRecord.config` (or to
398	  SettingsRecord — see decision).
399	- `docs/SETUP_IOS.md` — new: mkcert walkthrough.
400	
401	### Acceptance criteria
402	- Phone on a coffee table at rest emits **zero** commit events for 60
403	  seconds.
404	- Phone strapped to wrist or held: a sharp forward-snap motion emits
405	  exactly one commit event within 50ms of the impulse peak.
406	- Calibration screen captures 5 samples and persists the threshold;
407	  re-running calibration overwrites the prior value.
408	- Android: works over HTTP without prompts (Chrome doesn't gate
409	  `devicemotion`).
410	- iOS: with mkcert HTTPS, "Tap to enable motion" grants permission
411	  and commits flow.
412	- Documented in `docs/SETUP_IOS.md`; iOS acceptance is doc-driven, not
413	  CI-driven.
414	
415	### Open technical decisions
416	- **Per-profile vs per-settings threshold**: a single athlete has one
417	  body; settings-singleton is simpler. But the "per-athlete" wording
418	  in `docs/PHASES.md` suggests profile-level. **Recommend
419	  per-profile** — the user already has multi-profile (Phase 4), so
420	  this composes. Profiles that don't have a calibration fall back to
421	  a sensible default (e.g. `thresholdG: 1.8` — a moderate impulse).
422	- **Impulse metric**: simplest is `max(|a| - g)` over a 200ms sliding
423	  window. More sophisticated is to compute jerk (numeric derivative)
424	  and threshold *that*. Start simple; revise if false-positives are
425	  too frequent in real-device QA.
426	- **Debounce**: once a commit fires, ignore further events for 300ms
427	  to avoid double-trigger from the recoil.
428	
429	### Test strategy
430	- `motion.test.ts`: pure-function tests on the impulse metric and
431	  threshold-crossing logic. Feed synthesized accel streams (still
432	  baseline, one impulse, double-tap, calibration sequence) and
433	  assert expected commit timestamps.
434	- Calibration math: feed 5 sample peakG values, assert resulting
435	  threshold matches `p10 - epsilon`.
436	- qa-playwright: cannot generate fake `devicemotion` easily — mark as
437	  manual real-device step.
438	- Real-device QA: documented script in verify-phase-2b.mjs (analogous
439	  to verify-phase4.mjs):
440	  1. Connect phone.
441	  2. Set phone on table → no commits in 30s.
442	  3. Punch motion × 5 → exactly 5 commits.
443	  4. Run calibration → threshold persists across reload.
444	
445	### Risks and mitigations
446	- *iOS user can't get mkcert working*: the doc is detailed; if they
447	  give up they can still use keyboard/pedal. Phone-as-sensor is
448	  marked as an optional input source in the spec.
449	- *Motion thresholds vary wildly by phone hardware*: the per-profile
450	  calibration captures this; the default is a fallback, not a claim.
451	- *Multiple commits per intended punch*: the 300ms debounce + jerk-
452	  rather-than-peak metric should mitigate. Tunable from Settings.
453	
454	### Rollback
455	The motion code is gated behind the phone input source. Reverting to
456	the 2b.2 shape leaves the "Send commit" button as a manual fallback;
457	calibration screen is hidden.
458	
459	---
460	
461	## Sub-phase 2b.4 — Wire `inputSource = 'phone'` into engine + session metadata
462	
463	### Scope
464	- Add `'phone'` to the `InputSource` union (`app/src/engine/types.ts:44`).
465	- Settings UI: add `<option value="phone">Phone (motion)</option>` to
466	  the input-source select.
467	- IdleScreen: if `inputSource === 'phone'` and no DataChannel is
468	  connected, show a banner "Phone not paired — pair now" with a button.
469	  Disable Start if not paired.
470	- TrainerScreen: subscribe to the DataChannel; on receiving a
471	  `commit` message, call the same `recordPress(at)` function that
472	  keyboard/pedal already use.
473	- SummaryScreen: already shows `inputSource` — no change needed.
474	- Analytics (Phase 5): no change; `inputSource` is opaque to it.
475	
476	### Files to touch
477	- `app/src/engine/types.ts` — `InputSource = 'keyboard' | 'pedal' |
478	  'phone'`. Existing rep records remain compatible (the field is just
479	  a string).
480	- `app/src/store/session.ts` — `start()`'s `inputSource` arg already
481	  accepts the new value.
482	- `app/src/ui/SettingsScreen.tsx` — extend select options.
483	- `app/src/ui/IdleScreen.tsx` — pre-flight check for paired phone.
484	- `app/src/ui/TrainerScreen.tsx` — DataChannel subscription.
485	- `app/src/phone/peer.ts` — expose a singleton connection getter
486	  (`getPhonePeer()`) so multiple screens can subscribe.
487	
488	### Acceptance criteria
489	- User in Settings picks "Phone", lands on Idle.
490	- If unpaired: banner + pair button block Start.
491	- If paired: Start enabled, drill runs, phone commits drive reps.
492	- Saved `SessionRecord.inputSource === 'phone'`.
493	- All 105+ existing tests still pass. New tests cover the union-
494	  member addition and the IdleScreen pre-flight gate.
495	
496	### Open technical decisions
497	- **Where does the singleton peer live?** Either Zustand store or a
498	  module-level singleton in `phone/peer.ts`. Recommend
499	  module-singleton with a small React hook (`usePhonePeer()`) for
500	  components; mirrors how `getDb()` works today.
501	- **What happens if the DataChannel drops mid-session?** Pause the
502	  drill, banner "Phone disconnected — reconnect to continue", same
503	  as a pedal unplug would feel.
504	- **Backward compat for old `SessionRecord.inputSource`**: existing
505	  rows have `'keyboard' | 'pedal'`; the type widening to include
506	  `'phone'` is purely additive. No migration.
507	
508	### Test strategy
509	- `session.test.ts`: extend the existing inputSource test to cover
510	  `'phone'`.
511	- `SettingsScreen` test: select "phone", verify settings persist.
512	- `IdleScreen` test: when inputSource is 'phone' and `getPhonePeer()`
513	  returns disconnected, Start is disabled.
514	- qa-playwright: full pair → calibrate → drill → summary flow.
515	  Acknowledge real-device dependency in the verify artifact.
516	
517	### Rollback
518	The `'phone'` literal is removed from the `InputSource` union;
519	existing rows with `inputSource: 'phone'` would type-error on read.
520	Mitigation: keep the type as `'keyboard' | 'pedal' | 'phone' |
521	string` for one version if we ever roll back, or use a string cast
522	at the read boundary. Realistically, Phase 2b lands together or
523	not at all.
524	
525	---
526	
527	## Risks and mitigations (cross-cutting)
528	
529	- **WebRTC is harder to test than HTTP.** Mitigation: keep transport
530	  logic in pure-ish modules (`peer.ts`, `wire.ts`, `motion.ts`) that
531	  vitest can exercise; reserve full pairing for manual real-device
532	  QA documented in `verify-phase-2b*.mjs`.
533	- **iOS HTTPS friction.** Mitigation: ship Android-only acceptance;
534	  doc-driven iOS support; do not block Phase 2b on iOS.
535	- **Bundle bloat from QR libraries.** Mitigation: `React.lazy` around
536	  PairScreen so the pairing modules only download when needed.
537	- **The phone goes to sleep mid-drill.** Mitigation: PhoneApp requests
538	  `screen.wakeLock` while a DataChannel is open. Falls back gracefully
539	  on browsers without the API (Safari < 16.4).
540	- **A red-team flag: a remote attacker on the same Wi-Fi could connect
541	  to the laptop's `/phone` endpoint and inject spurious commits.**
542	  Mitigation: the QR-distributed offer SDP carries a per-session
543	  random nonce; the laptop only accepts a DataChannel whose answer
544	  references that nonce. This is light auth, not a security boundary —
545	  the threat model is "annoyance," not "attacker on hostile network."
546	- **Phase 5 analytics breakage:** `inputSource = 'phone'` may surface
547	  in trend rows. Verify the analytics text labels handle the new value
548	  (probably already do; the field is opaque to most analytics math).
549	
550	## Test strategy summary
551	
552	Per sub-phase the unit/vitest layer covers all pure logic (wire format,
553	QR encode/decode, peer wrapper, motion impulse detection, calibration
554	math, IdleScreen gate). The manual real-device layer covers the
555	end-to-end pairing and motion-trigger paths; each sub-phase ships a
556	verify script + manual QA checklist (mirroring `verify-phase4.mjs`).
557	
558	qa-playwright tests cover everything *except* WebRTC handshake and
559	`devicemotion` (browsers under test don't provide either reliably).
560	These are documented as a known limitation in the verify artifact.
561	
562	## Acceptance criteria for the next implementation step (2b.1)
563	
564	- New `/phone` route exists; visiting it on a phone on the same Wi-Fi
565	  renders `PhoneApp`.
566	- Laptop "Pair phone" screen produces an offer SDP textarea.
567	- Manual copy/paste of offer onto phone + answer onto laptop establishes
568	  a DataChannel within 5 seconds (in a real-device QA run).
569	- Pressing the phone's "Send commit" button echoes a `commit` message
570	  the laptop displays with a timestamp.
571	- `SettingsRecord` carries a new optional `laptopLanIp` field.
572	- All 105 existing tests pass. New unit tests for `wire.ts` and
573	  `peer.ts` (the parts that don't need real `RTCPeerConnection`).
574	- Lint + tsc + vite build clean; bundle growth budget +20 KB gzip.
575	- Documented manual QA steps in `app/verify-phase-2b1.mjs` (new).
576	- `docs/PHASES.md` updated to add 2b.1–2b.4 (a separate, builder-
577	  driven edit — this memo is the input).
578	
579	## Out-of-scope (explicitly deferred past 2b.4)
580	
581	- Multi-phone support (one phone per laptop, one DataChannel at a time).
582	- Phone-driven UI for selecting drills (the spec marks phone as sensor
583	  only, not primary UI).
584	- Auto-reconnect on transient drops (manual re-pair only).
585	- iOS-on-HTTP support (requires Apple to change Safari).
586	- Cloud signaling fallback (would break local-first guarantee).
587	- Pose-based commit detection (Phase 7).
